overview: Operators are the symbols that combine values into expressions: arithmetic (+, -, *, /, %), comparison (==, !=, <, >, <=, >=), logical (&&, ||, !), and bitwise (&, |, ^, &^, <<, >>) operators.
An expression is any code that evaluates to a value; Go's operators are strongly typed, so both operands of a binary operator must usually be the same type, and there are no implicit conversions.
Go intentionally keeps the operator set small and removes footguns from C: no operator overloading, no comma operator, and increment/decrement (++/--) are statements, not expressions.
learningObjectives: Use Go's arithmetic, comparison, logical, and bitwise operators correctly with proper types.
Understand operator precedence and how Go differs from C (five precedence levels, ++ as a statement).
Apply short-circuit evaluation of && and || and avoid common pitfalls.
Use bitwise operators including Go's unique AND-NOT (&^) operator.
coreConcept.formalDefinition: In Go, an operator is a symbol that performs a computation on one or more operands to produce a value; an expression is a syntactic construct that, when evaluated, yields a value, governed by Go's typing rules (matching operand types, no implicit conversion) and a simplified five-tier operator precedence.
coreConcept.simpleExplanation: Operators are the math and logic symbols you use to compute things — add numbers, compare them, combine true/false values, or flip bits. In Go, the operands you combine must be the same type (you can't add an int and a float64 without converting), and a few things that are tricky in other languages — like ++ — are simplified so they can only be used as standalone statements.
coreConcept.historicalContext: Go's operators derive from C, but the designers deliberately simplified them: C's 15 precedence levels were reduced to 5 (making expressions easier to read without memorizing a big table), ++ and -- were made statements to avoid expression-position bugs, and the unusual &^ (AND NOT / bit clear) operator was added for clean bit manipulation. This has been stable since Go 1.0 (2012).

whyItMatters.business: Correct, readable expressions reduce subtle logic bugs that cause incorrect results and costly incidents.
whyItMatters.engineering: A small operator set and clear precedence make code easier to read and review, lowering cognitive load.
whyItMatters.scalability: Bitwise operations enable compact flag/permission handling and fast computations used throughout high-scale systems.
whyItMatters.cost: Avoiding integer-overflow and division-by-zero bugs prevents production failures and the cost of fixing corrupted data.
whyItMatters.reliability: Short-circuit evaluation and strict typing prevent nil-dereference and type-mismatch bugs before they reach production.

internalWorking: Binary operators require operands of the same type (with untyped constants adapting); mixing typed int and float64 is a compile error without an explicit conversion.
Go uses five precedence levels for binary operators (highest to lowest): * / % << >> & &^, then + - | ^, then == != < <= > >=, then &&, then ||.
Integer division truncates toward zero and % is the remainder with the sign of the dividend; dividing an integer by zero panics at runtime.
&& and || short-circuit: the right operand is only evaluated if the result isn't already determined by the left, which is commonly used for safe nil checks.
++ and -- are statements, so you cannot write `x = a++` or use them inside expressions; this removes a whole class of C-style sequence-point bugs.
coreConcept.architectureFlow: expression --> [type-check operands match] --> [apply precedence to parse subexpressions] --> [evaluate left-to-right, short-circuiting &&/||] --> resulting value (with runtime checks like divide-by-zero)
dataFlowWalkthrough: You write a condition like `n > 0 && data[n-1] == target`.
The compiler checks operand types (n and 0 are ints; the comparison yields bool).
At runtime, `n > 0` is evaluated first; if false, the right side is skipped (short-circuit), avoiding an out-of-range index.
The combined boolean drives the control flow.

importantConcepts.concept: Integer vs float division and modulo
importantConcepts.explanation: / truncates for integers and % only applies to integers; for fractional results convert to float64 first. Division by zero panics for integers but yields +Inf/NaN for floats.
They stand alone (i++) and can't appear inside expressions, so there's no pre/post-increment ambiguity as in C.

tradeOffs.whenToUse: Use arithmetic/comparison/logical operators for everyday logic, short-circuiting for safe guards, and bitwise operators for compact flags and performance-sensitive bit manipulation.
tradeOffs.whenToAvoid: Avoid relying on operator overloading (Go has none), avoid integer division when you need fractions, and avoid clever precedence tricks — add parentheses for clarity.

coreConcept.realWorldAnalogy: Operators are like the buttons on a calculator, and precedence is the built-in rule that it does multiplication before addition. Short-circuit evaluation is like a careful inspector who, once a checklist item fails (the left condition is false for &&), stops checking the rest because the outcome is already decided — saving work and avoiding poking at something (like a nil pointer) that shouldn't be touched.

codeExamples.title: Arithmetic, comparison, logical, and short-circuiting
codeExamples.overview: Show integer vs float division, modulo, comparisons, and how short-circuit evaluation guards a slice index.
codeExamples.breakdown: 7/2 truncates to 3 and 7%2 is the remainder 1. To get 3.5 you must convert both operands to float64. Comparisons return bool. The if uses `len(nums) > 0 && nums[0] == 1`: because len is 0, the left operand is false and Go short-circuits, never evaluating nums[0], so there's no index-out-of-range panic. Finally `count++` is a standalone statement.
codeExamples.expectedOutput:
7/2 = 3 7%2 = 1
7/2 as float = 3.5
a > b: true a == b: false
empty or first != 1
count: 1
codeExamples.commonIssues: Expecting 7/2 to be 3.5 (it's integer division), writing `x := count++` (++ isn't an expression), or putting the index check before the length check (loses the short-circuit guard).
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Order && conditions so the cheapest/most-decisive check is first; convert to float64 only when a fractional result is truly needed.

codeExamples.title: Bitwise operators including AND-NOT (&^)
codeExamples.overview: Set, test, clear, and toggle bits using &, |, ^, and Go's &^ operator on a flag set.
codeExamples.code:
package main

import "fmt"

type Flags uint8

const (
	Read  Flags = 1 << iota // 1
	Write                   // 2
	Exec                    // 4
)

func main() {
	var f Flags

	f |= Read | Write          // SET Read and Write bits -> 011
	fmt.Printf("set:    %03b\n", f)

	fmt.Println("has Write:", f&Write != 0) // TEST a bit

	f &^= Write                // CLEAR the Write bit using AND-NOT -> 001
	fmt.Printf("cleared:%04b\n", f)

	f ^= Exec                  // TOGGLE the Exec bit on -> 101
	fmt.Printf("toggled:%03b\n", f)

	// Shifts: multiply/divide by powers of two.
	n := 3
	fmt.Println("3<<2 =", n<<2, "  3>>1 =", n>>1) // 12 and 1
}
codeExamples.breakdown: `f |= Read | Write` sets two bits with OR. `f & Write != 0` tests whether a bit is set. `f &^= Write` uses the AND-NOT operator to clear the Write bit in one step (equivalent to f & ^Write). `f ^= Exec` toggles the Exec bit with XOR. Left shift `n<<2` multiplies by 4 (3->12) and right shift `n>>1` integer-divides by 2 (3->1).
codeExamples.expectedOutput:
set:    011
has Write: true
cleared:0001
toggled:101
3<<2 = 12   3>>1 = 1
codeExamples.commonIssues: Confusing &^ (clear) with & (test), forgetting that shift counts must be non-negative, or assuming XOR sets a bit (it toggles it).
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Use &^ to clear flags cleanly instead of f & ^mask; prefer shifts over multiply/divide by powers of two only when it improves clarity, since the compiler optimizes both.

endToEndExample.businessProblem: A rate-limiting feature must compute time buckets and check combined permission flags efficiently, after a past bug where integer division and a non-short-circuited nil check caused crashes.
endToEndExample.inputData: Request timestamps (int64 seconds), a bucket size, and per-user permission flag sets.
endToEndExample.architecture: Arithmetic with explicit types for bucketing, short-circuited guards for nil/empty checks, and bitwise operators for permission flags.
processingSteps: Compute bucket = timestamp / bucketSize using integer division (intended truncation).
Compute offset = timestamp % bucketSize for position within the bucket.
Guard lookups with `user != nil && user.Flags&Write != 0` so a nil user short-circuits safely.
Combine and clear permission flags with | and &^.
Validate bucketSize != 0 before dividing to avoid a panic.
endToEndExample.output: Correct time buckets and safe, efficient permission checks with no division-by-zero or nil-dereference panics.
endToEndExample.monitoring: Track denied requests by flag and alert on unexpected division-guard hits (bucketSize == 0).
endToEndExample.errorHandling: Reject bucketSize == 0 before dividing; the nil guard prevents dereferencing a missing user.
endToEndExample.finalResult: Intentional integer truncation for buckets, short-circuited guards preventing crashes, and bitwise flag handling deliver a correct, efficient rate limiter.

beginnerQuestions.question: What does the % operator do and what types does it work on?
beginnerQuestions.answer: It computes the integer remainder of division and works only on integers (the result takes the sign of the dividend).

beginnerQuestions.question: Why is `i++` not usable inside an expression in Go?
beginnerQuestions.answer: Because ++ and -- are statements in Go, not expressions, so they must appear on their own.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Checks awareness of a key Go/C difference.

intermediateQuestions.question: How does short-circuit evaluation help avoid panics?
intermediateQuestions.answer: For &&, if the left operand is false the right isn't evaluated; placing a guard like len(s)>0 or p!=nil first prevents evaluating a risky index or dereference.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Tests practical use of logical operators.

intermediateQuestions.question: What is the &^ operator and when do you use it?
intermediateQuestions.answer: &^ is AND-NOT (bit clear): a &^ b clears the bits in a that are set in b, used to remove flags cleanly.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Probes knowledge of Go's unique bitwise operator.

advancedQuestions.question: Explain Go's operator precedence and how it differs from C.
advancedQuestions.answer: Go has five binary precedence levels (highest to lowest: * / % << >> & &^; then + - | ^; then comparisons; then &&; then ||), far fewer than C's many levels, making expressions easier to read.

advancedQuestions.question: What happens on integer divide-by-zero versus float divide-by-zero in Go?
advancedQuestions.answer: Integer division by zero causes a runtime panic, whereas float64 division by zero yields +Inf, -Inf, or NaN per IEEE-754.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Assesses understanding of runtime arithmetic behavior.

scenarioBasedQuestions.scenario: A service occasionally panics with 'index out of range' inside a condition that checks the first element of a slice.
scenarioBasedQuestions.thinkingProcess: The condition likely evaluates the index before checking length, so short-circuiting can't protect it.
scenarioBasedQuestions.expectedAnswer: Reorder to `len(s) > 0 && s[0] == x` so the length guard short-circuits the index access when the slice is empty.

systemDesignQuestions.tradeOffs: Bitsets are compact and fast but limited by integer width; explicit checks are clearer than implicit truthiness.
systemDesignQuestions.scalingStrategy: Use a wide unsigned type for growth, cache computed flag masks, and keep checks O(1).

cheatSheet.oneLineDefinition: Operators combine operands into expressions; Go offers arithmetic, comparison, logical (short-circuiting), and bitwise operators with strict typing and only five precedence levels.
keyConcepts: Operands of binary operators must share a type (no implicit conversion).
Integer / truncates and % is integer-only; int divide-by-zero panics.
&^ is AND-NOT (bit clear), unique to Go.
formulas: x << n == x * 2^n ;  x >> n == x / 2^n (for non-negative ints)
commands: q, r := a/b, a%b // integer quotient and remainder
ok := p != nil && p.Valid // short-circuit guard
f |= Write ; f &^= Write ; f ^= Exec // set, clear, toggle
has := f & Read != 0 // test a bit
interviewPoints: &^ clears bits; no ternary, no operator overloading.
quickNotes: Convert to float64 for fractional division.

keyTakeaways: Go's operators (arithmetic, comparison, logical, bitwise) are strongly typed: operands must match and there are no implicit conversions.
Logical && and || short-circuit, which you should exploit to guard nil and bounds checks; ++ and -- are statements, not expressions.
Integer division truncates and % is integer-only, with integer divide-by-zero panicking — convert to float64 for fractional results.
Bitwise operators, including Go's unique &^ (AND-NOT/clear), enable compact flag handling, and Go's five precedence levels keep expressions readable.
